### Contiguous Dominants

Dominant 7th chords may also move by **half-step** or **whole-step** for chromatic dominant motion.
These are called contiguous dominants (or parallel dominants) and create tension through
chromatic voice leading.

**Half-step approach (subdominant / tritone sub motion):**

- **D♭7 → Cmaj7** — D♭7 is a half step above the tonic, resolving by step

**Whole-step approach:**

- **A7 → G7 → Cmaj7** — A7 moves down a whole step to G7

**Chromatic descending dominant chain:**

- **B♭7 – A7 – A♭7 – G7 → Cmaj7** — four dominant chords descending by half step

This type of motion appears frequently in jazz arrangements and reharmonisations because
each dominant creates tension and the chromatic descent provides smooth voice leading.

An upper-structure triad (UST) is a simple major or minor triad played above a bass note (or 7th-chord shell) to highlight specific colour tones — the tensions that distinguish one chord-scale from another.
A 7th chord typically spells only four notes: root, 3rd, 5th, and 7th. The remaining scale degrees (9, 11, 13 and their alterations) are the tensions that give each mode its characteristic sound.
Superimposing a triad built on one of those tensions efficiently delivers two or three colour tones at once. The underlying chord supplies the guide tones; the upper triad supplies the colour.
The upper triad does not always spell a complete mode by itself. It highlights the characteristic tensions while the rhythm-section harmony provides the remaining tones.
A major triad built on the 2nd degree (II) supplies 9, ♯11, and 13 — the three colour tones that distinguish Lydian from plain major.
See also: Lydian mode
A major triad built on the ♭7th degree (♭VII) provides ♭7, 9, and 11 — the suspended dominant or Mixolydian sound.
See also: Mixolydian mode
A major triad built on ♭II supplies ♭9, 11, and ♭13 — the dark Phrygian or pedal-point colour.
See also: Phrygian mode

A shell chord is a voicing that uses only the essential guide tones — the 3rd and 7th — omitting the root and fifth. These two notes define the chord's quality and voice leading direction.
The root and fifth are implied by context (bass line, other instruments).
The tritone between the 3rd and 7th of a dominant chord (V7) is what drives resolution to I. When the V7 resolves:
The 3rd resolves up by a half step to the root of I
The 7th resolves down by a half step to the 3rd of I
This half-step voice leading is the engine of harmonic motion.
A dominant 7th chord can be replaced by the dominant chord a tritone away (6 semitones). Both chords share the same guide tones (3rd and 7th are enharmonic).

Why shells are central in jazz
On a ii–V–I, shell tones move with very small intervals (often common tone or half-step), which creates smooth voice leading.
Only one note changes at a time in each step.
A suspended chord replaces the 3rd with either a 2nd or 4th.
Because the 3rd is missing, suspended chords delay the clear major/minor quality.
In jazz and fusion, the most common suspended color is 7sus4 (and extensions like 9sus4):
This sound often resolves to a regular dominant by moving 4 → 3 while keeping the rest of the harmony stable.
Suspended dominants are frequently voiced as slash chords.
Example: C7sus4(9) can be heard as B♭/C (B♭ major triad over C bass).
This links sus harmony to modal colors, especially Phrygian and Mixolydian contexts where the suspended 4th is central.
An extended chord starts with a 7th chord and keeps stacking thirds above it. Once the stack goes past the octave, the new chord tones are named 9th, 11th, and 13th instead of 2nd, 4th, and 6th.
In strict tertian theory, a higher extension implies the lower ones below it. In real voicings, players often omit tones that are less essential.
The 3rd and 7th still define the chord quality and function. Those guide tones tell you whether the chord is major, dominant, or minor.
The 5th is often optional, and the 11th is commonly omitted on many 13th voicings because it can muddy the sound or clash with the 3rd.
Rootless voicings omit the root and keep the color tones that define function and movement.
A voicing and B voicing are two fixed 4-note layouts used for major, dominant, minor, and half-diminished chords.
They are commonly split as LH = lower two notes and RH = upper two notes.
In a rhythm section, the bass covers the root, so piano can focus on guide tones and extensions.
Rootless A/B voicings are central to jazz comping because they produce compact, reusable shapes and very smooth voice leading through functional progressions.
When to use A vs B
Use either as a stable comping shape for one chord quality.
Alternate A and B to keep motion compact through progressions.
A classic major-key line is ii (A) → V (B) → I (A).
The ii-V-I progression is the backbone of jazz harmony. Every jazz standard uses it in some form.
Minor key (e.g. C minor — harmonic minor for V7)
The raised 7th of harmonic minor creates a leading tone and a natural V7 chord.
Backcycling (also called back-cycling or chain of dominants) extends a cadence by prepending earlier dominant approaches. Each new dominant resolves to the next chord in the chain.
The process works backwards through the circle of fifths: each new dominant is a P5 above (or P4 below) the previous target.

Each ii-V pair tonicises the chord that follows it. The chain can be extended as far as desired.
Key insight: The dominant cycle follows the circle of fifths backwards — each new V7 is a perfect fifth above the previous ii.

Dominant 7th chords may also move by half-step or whole-step for chromatic dominant motion. These are called contiguous dominants (or parallel dominants) and create tension through chromatic voice leading.
D♭7 → Cmaj7 — D♭7 is a half step above the tonic, resolving by step
A7 → G7 → Cmaj7 — A7 moves down a whole step to G7
B♭7 – A7 – A♭7 – G7 → Cmaj7 — four dominant chords descending by half step
This type of motion appears frequently in jazz arrangements and reharmonisations because each dominant creates tension and the chromatic descent provides smooth voice leading.
A tension is a note added to a 7th chord beyond the four basic chord tones. Tensions create color and motion.
Not all tensions sound good on every chord. A tension is available if it does not create a dissonant half-step (minor 9th) against any chord tone.
An avoid note is a note that creates this half-step clash — it sounds unresolved or wrong when sustained.
Dominant chords (the V chord) have the most available tensions because their function is to create tension that resolves to I.
Non-dominant chords (major 7, minor 7, etc.) have fewer available tensions because they need to remain stable:
Maj7: 9, #11, 13 (avoid the natural 11 — it clashes with the major 3rd)
m7: 9, 11 (avoid the major 6th / natural 13th in most contexts)

On a Maj7 chord in a major key, the natural 4th (11th) is only a half step above the 3rd. Sustained, it creates tension that doesn't resolve — so it's treated as an avoid note in most contexts (though it can be used as a passing tone).
